original_value: AbstractThe use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) as a feature learning method for Human Activity Recognition (HAR) is becoming more and more common. Unlike conventional machine learning methods, which require domain-specific expertise, CNNs can extract features automatically. On the other hand, CNNs require a training phase, making them prone to the cold-start problem. In this work, a case study is presented where the use of a pre-trained CNN feature extractor is evaluated under realistic conditions. The case study consists of two main steps: (1) different topologies and parameters are assessed to identify the best candidate models for HAR, thus obtaining a pre-trained CNN model. The pre-trained model (2) is then employed as feature extractor evaluating its use with a large scale real-world dataset. Two CNN applications were considered: Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) and audio based HAR. For the IMU data, balanced accuracy was 91.98% on the UCI-HAR dataset, and 67.51% on the real-world Extrasensory dataset. For the audio data, the balanced accuracy was 92.30% on the DCASE 2017 dataset, and 35.24% on the Extrasensory dataset.

result.paraphrase: Abstract: The application of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for feature learning in Human Activity Recognition (HAR) is increasingly widespread. In contrast to traditional machine learning approaches that depend on domain knowledge, CNNs can automatically learn features. However, because they need a training stage, CNNs are susceptible to the cold-start problem. This paper presents a case study that examines a pre-trained CNN feature extractor under realistic conditions. The study has two main phases: first, various topologies and parameters are evaluated to select the most suitable HAR candidate models, producing a pre-trained CNN model; second, that model is used as a feature extractor and tested on a large-scale real-world dataset. Two CNN-based HAR scenarios were analyzed: Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) data and audio data. For the IMU case, balanced accuracy reached 91.98% on the UCI-HAR dataset and 67.51% on the real-world Extrasensory dataset. For the audio case, balanced accuracy was 92.30% on the DCASE 2017 dataset and 35.24% on the Extrasensory dataset.
